body.text: Overview and Empirical Foundations of Ice age

Most coverage of Ice age misses the structural details that actually matter in science. When you look closely at real-world evidence, clear patterns emerge that separate durable results from short-term noise.
What makes Ice age one of the most revealing subjects in empirical research? Primary observations and reproducible data continue to reshape how scientists model the physical world.

An ice age is a period of time when decreased temperature of Earth's surface and atmosphere results in the prolonged presence or expansion of continental alpine glaciers and polar ice caps. The term is applied in several different senses to very long and comparatively short periods of cooling.
An ice age may consist of numerous sub-periods where the global temperature and glaciation fluctuates, with the colder periods called glacials, and relatively warmer periods called interglacials.

Earth's climate alternates between icehouse and greenhouse periods based on whether there are glaciers on the planet, and for most of Earth's history it has been in a greenhouse period with little or no permanent ice.
Over the very long term, Earth is currently in an icehouse period called the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, which started 34 million years ago.
Within this period, the Last Interglacial ended 115,000 years ago, and was followed by the Last Glacial Period (LGP), which gave way to the current warm Holocene, which started 11,700 years ago.
